concepts.def: Any named group of organisms in a classification, at any level; the plural is taxa. In the traditional hierarchy every organism belongs to one taxon at each rank, from kingdom down to species, and each taxon at one rank is contained within a single taxon of the rank above.

The ranked series kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species, in which each rank is nested within the one above. The hierarchy was constructed largely from morphology before evolutionary relationships were known, so it does not always correspond to patterns of divergence generated by evolution. A fixed ranking is also arbitrary, because there is no natural criterion that makes a family in one group equivalent to a family in another: the ranks are imposed on a gradation of variation.

An approach to classification in which organisms are grouped into clades on the basis of shared common ancestry, deduced most objectively from base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins. Clades are unranked: they nest inside one another to any depth and are not assigned to kingdom, phylum, class or any other fixed rank. Cladistics offers an alternative to the traditional ranked hierarchy rather than a redrawing of it.

A change in the fundamental framework of assumptions and methods within which a science is practised, rather than a refinement of details inside the existing framework. The replacement of classification by fixed ranks with classification by unranked clades, defined by common ancestry, is an example of the paradigm shift that sometimes occurs in scientific theories.

The ideal classification, in which every taxonomic group consists of organisms that have all evolved from a common ancestor, so that the groups mirror the branching pattern of evolution. Its advantage is predictive: because characteristics are shared within a clade, the characteristics of an organism can be predicted from the group it belongs to, including characteristics that have not yet been studied in that species.

A species from which two or more later species have descended. All the members of a group in an evolutionary classification share a common ancestor that is not shared with organisms outside the group, and the characteristics inherited from that ancestor are what the members have in common.

The method of estimating when two clades diverged from a common ancestor from the number of differences between their base sequences or amino acid sequences, on the basis that sequence differences accumulate gradually over time in each lineage. Both lineages accumulate changes after they separate, so the differences between two living species are shared between the two lineages. The clock can only give estimates, because mutation rates are affected by the length of the generation time, the size of a population, the intensity of selective pressure and other factors.

A branching tree diagram that shows the most probable pattern of divergence of a set of organisms into clades, constructed from base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins (or, less objectively, from morphological traits). A cladogram is a hypothesis about evolutionary relationships: different genes or different criteria for judgement can lead to different cladograms for the same organisms.

The criterion used to select the most probable cladogram from the alternatives: the cladogram in which the observed sequence variation between clades is accounted for with the smallest number of sequence changes is chosen. The number of changes is totalled over all positions in the sequences, so a tree favoured by one position may be rejected because it needs more changes at others.

The base of a cladogram, representing the common ancestor of all the organisms shown. Every lineage on the cladogram descends from the root, so all the living organisms at the tips have been evolving for the same length of time since it.

A branching point on a cladogram, representing a hypothetical common ancestor of the lineages that arise from it. The node is inferred from the data, not an identified fossil or a living species. All the organisms on the branches beyond a node form a clade, and the more recent the node at which two organisms' lineages join, the more closely related they are. Branches can be rotated about a node without changing the relationships shown.

A branch of a cladogram that ends at one of the organisms or groups being compared, rather than at a further node. The left-to-right order of terminal branches carries no information about relatedness, and a terminal branch far from the root does not represent a more advanced organism.

The independent evolution of similar characteristics in lineages that do not share a recent common ancestor, usually because they are subject to similar selective pressures. Similarities due to convergent evolution can suggest a classification that groups unrelated organisms together; cladistic analysis of base sequences can show such a classification to be false, as happened with the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae), which was defined by floral morphology and from which several genera were transferred to other families.

The rejection of a theory or other scientific knowledge claim when it is contradicted by evidence. A classification is a knowledge claim about evolutionary relationships and may eventually be falsified: cladistics tests whether the members of a named group form a clade, and where they do not, as in the traditional figwort family, the classification is revised.

The highest taxonomic level, introduced above the kingdoms in the reclassification proposed in 1977. Each domain contains one or more kingdoms, so the domains added an extra level to the hierarchy rather than replacing the kingdoms.

concepts.term: Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya
concepts.def: The three groups into which all organisms are classified. Bacteria and Archaea are both prokaryotic, but their rRNA base sequences are as different from each other as either is from Eukarya, so they are separate domains. Eukarya contains all eukaryotes, including the plant, animal and fungal kingdoms. The three-way division was proposed in 1977 by Carl Woese and colleagues from rRNA sequence comparisons; the term domain and the current names were adopted later.

RNA that forms part of the structure of ribosomes in every organism. Because all organisms have ribosomes, and because rRNA genes change only slowly, their base sequences can be compared across the whole of life. Comparison of rRNA base sequences was the evidence used to propose the three domains: it revealed that prokaryotes fall into two groups, Bacteria and Archaea, that are not distinguishable by cell structure but are deeply separated in sequence.

mcqs.q: Two taxonomists disagree about whether a group of beetles should be ranked as a family or as a subfamily. Which statement best explains why such disagreements arise?
options: One of the two taxonomists must be wrong, because the rank of a group is a fixed natural property.
The ranks are arbitrary levels imposed on a continuous gradation of variation among organisms.
The beetles cannot be a natural group, because a true clade fits exactly one rank.
A cladogram of the beetles would settle the question by assigning the clade its correct rank.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the ranked hierarchy does not fit evolution
mcqs.explain: A fixed ranking of taxa is arbitrary because it does not reflect the gradation of variation. Two taxonomists can draw the family boundary at different levels with equal justification, which is one reason cladistics uses unranked clades.
rationales: A student who thinks ranks exist in nature picks this. There is no natural criterion that fixes whether a group is a family or a subfamily; the disagreement arises precisely because the rank is a convention, not a measurable property.

A fixed ranking of taxa is arbitrary because it does not reflect the gradation of variation. Two taxonomists can draw the family boundary at different levels with equal justification, which is one reason cladistics uses unranked clades.

A student who assumes traditional taxa and evolutionary groups always coincide picks this. Whether the beetles form a clade is a separate question from what rank to give them; a clade can be given any rank or none.

A student who thinks cladistics is the ranked hierarchy drawn as a tree picks this. Cladistics uses unranked clades: a cladogram can show that the beetles form a clade, but it does not and cannot say whether that clade is a family.

mcqs.q: Cladistics classifies organisms into unranked clades. Why is the change from the traditional ranked hierarchy to cladistics described as a paradigm shift?
options: It draws the same ranked hierarchy of kingdom, phylum and class in a new, tree-shaped form.
It replaces hypotheses with facts, because cladograms are built from DNA sequence data.
It replaces the assumption of fixed ranks with a different framework of nested clades.
It provides a way of measuring the true rank of every group of organisms.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the ranked hierarchy does not fit evolution
mcqs.explain: A paradigm shift is a change in the underlying framework of a science. Cladistics discards the assumption that organisms fall into fixed ranks and instead groups them into unranked clades defined by common ancestry, which is a different way of thinking about classification rather than a refinement of the old one.
rationales: A student who merges cladistics with the Linnaean hierarchy picks this. If cladistics only redrew the same ranks, it would be a change of presentation, not a paradigm shift; in fact it abandons fixed ranks altogether.

A student who takes cladograms to be proven facts picks this. A cladogram is a hypothesis selected by parsimony, and different criteria can lead to different hypotheses; the shift is in the framework, not from hypothesis to fact.

A paradigm shift is a change in the underlying framework of a science. Cladistics discards the assumption that organisms fall into fixed ranks and instead groups them into unranked clades defined by common ancestry, which is a different way of thinking about classification rather than a refinement of the old one.

A student who believes ranks are real properties waiting to be measured picks this. Cladistics does not measure ranks; it does away with them, because a fixed ranking is arbitrary and does not reflect the gradation of variation.

mcqs.q: A newly discovered plant species is placed, on the basis of DNA base sequences, in a clade in which every known member produces a particular alkaloid. What can be concluded about the new species?
options: It will resemble the other members in appearance, because that is how the clade was defined.
Nothing can be predicted until its morphology has been compared with that of the others.
Only its DNA sequence is known to match the others; no other trait can be inferred.
It is likely to produce the alkaloid, a trait shared by descent within the clade.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why grouping by ancestry is the ideal
mcqs.explain: This is the advantage of a classification that corresponds to evolutionary relationships: characteristics of organisms within a clade can be predicted because they are shared within the clade, having been inherited from the common ancestor. The prediction is probable rather than certain, since the trait could have been lost in one lineage.
rationales: A student who thinks classification is by appearance picks this. The clade was defined by common ancestry inferred from base sequences, not by appearance, and members of a clade can look very different from one another.

A student who trusts morphology over sequence data picks this. Base sequences are the most objective evidence for clade membership, and once membership is established the shared characteristics of the clade can be predicted without a morphological comparison.

A student who treats a clade as a loose group sharing only the trait used to define it picks this. A clade is a group descended from a common ancestor, so its members share many inherited characteristics beyond the sequence used to identify it.

This is the advantage of a classification that corresponds to evolutionary relationships: characteristics of organisms within a clade can be predicted because they are shared within the clade, having been inherited from the common ancestor. The prediction is probable rather than certain, since the trait could have been lost in one lineage.

mcqs.q: Birds and crocodiles share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with lizards. The traditional class Reptilia includes crocodiles and lizards but excludes birds. Which statement is correct?
options: Reptilia is a clade, because all of its members share scales and a similar body plan, unlike birds.
Traditional Reptilia is not a clade, because it omits some descendants of its common ancestor.
Reptilia is a clade, because it is an established class in the traditional hierarchy.
Birds cannot be grouped with crocodiles, because the two look so different from each other.
mcqs.specStatementText: A clade is an ancestor plus all its descendants
mcqs.explain: The common ancestor of crocodiles and lizards is also an ancestor of birds, since birds and crocodiles share a more recent ancestor than either does with lizards. A clade includes all descendants of the common ancestor, so a Reptilia that excludes birds is not a clade.
rationales: A student who thinks any group with shared characteristics is a clade picks this. A clade must contain all the descendants of its common ancestor; shared scales do not make up for leaving out the birds.

The common ancestor of crocodiles and lizards is also an ancestor of birds, since birds and crocodiles share a more recent ancestor than either does with lizards. A clade includes all descendants of the common ancestor, so a Reptilia that excludes birds is not a clade.

A student who assumes every traditional taxon is a natural group picks this. The traditional hierarchy does not always correspond to patterns of divergence generated by evolution, and Reptilia is a standard example of the mismatch.

A student who classifies by appearance picks this. Clades are defined by common ancestry, not resemblance; feathers and flight are later modifications in the bird lineage and do not alter its shared ancestry with crocodiles.

mcqs.q: In a comparison of one protein, species P and Q differ at 6 amino acid positions, P and R differ at 18, and Q and R differ at 18. Which conclusion is justified?
options: R has changed three times as much as P has since the two lineages separated from their common ancestor.
R is the most primitive of the three species, because its lineage was the first to diverge.
R's lineage separated from the lineage leading to P and Q before P and Q split from each other.
No order of divergence can be inferred until the morphology of the three species has been compared.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sequence differences accumulate, so they estimate divergence time
mcqs.explain: Sequence differences accumulate gradually with time, so the pair with the fewest differences, P and Q, diverged most recently, and R, which is equally distant from both, diverged from their shared lineage earlier. The clock gives only an estimate of the times, but the order is well supported.
rationales: A student who attributes all the differences to one species picks this. The 18 differences between P and R accumulated in both lineages since their common ancestor, so under a molecular clock P and R have each changed by a similar amount.

A student who reads early branching on a cladogram as primitiveness picks this. All three species have been evolving for the same length of time since their common ancestor; R's lineage separated earlier, which says nothing about how advanced it is.

Sequence differences accumulate gradually with time, so the pair with the fewest differences, P and Q, diverged most recently, and R, which is equally distant from both, diverged from their shared lineage earlier. The clock gives only an estimate of the times, but the order is well supported.

A student who regards morphology as more reliable than sequence data picks this. Amino acid sequence differences are the most objective evidence of relationship, and the gradual accumulation of differences is the basis for estimating the order and timing of divergence.

mcqs.q: Six bases of the same gene were sequenced in four species: W is ACTGCG, X is ACTATG, Y is GTAGCG and Z is GTAATG. Using parsimony analysis, which cladogram is the most probable?
options: W with X and Y with Z, because that tree accounts for all the variation with only 7 base changes.
W with Y and X with Z, because W and Y share the same bases at positions 4 and 5.
All four species branching from a single node, because that tree has the fewest nodes.
No cladogram can be chosen until the morphological traits of the four species are compared.
mcqs.explain: Positions 1, 2 and 3 each need one change if W is grouped with X and Y with Z, and positions 4 and 5 each need two changes, giving 7 in total (position 6 is invariant). Grouping W with Y and X with Z needs 8, and any other arrangement needs 10, so this is the most parsimonious hypothesis.
rationales: Positions 1, 2 and 3 each need one change if W is grouped with X and Y with Z, and positions 4 and 5 each need two changes, giving 7 in total (position 6 is invariant). Grouping W with Y and X with Z needs 8, and any other arrangement needs 10, so this is the most parsimonious hypothesis.

A student who builds the tree from the first shared pattern noticed picks this. Positions 4 and 5 do favour this grouping, but positions 1, 2 and 3 then each need two changes instead of one, so the tree needs 8 changes overall against 7 for the alternative.

A student who takes parsimony to mean the simplest-looking diagram picks this. Parsimony counts sequence changes, not nodes: a tree in which all four species arise from one node needs two changes at each of the five variable positions, 10 in all.

A student who regards sequence data as insufficient without morphology picks this. Base sequences are the most objective basis for constructing cladograms, and parsimony analysis selects the most probable tree from the sequence data alone.

mcqs.q: What does a node on a cladogram represent?
options: A named living or fossil species from which the later lineages are descended.
The point at which one lineage became more advanced than the other lineage.
The hypothetical common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it.
The taxonomic rank, such as family, shared by lineages beyond it.
mcqs.explain: A node represents a hypothetical common ancestor: the point at which the lineages arising from it diverged. All the organisms on the branches beyond a node form a clade.
rationales: A student who reads a cladogram like a family tree of named individuals picks this. The ancestor at a node is inferred from the data, not identified; living species appear only at the ends of terminal branches.
A student who sees a cladogram as a ladder of progress picks this. A node is a branching point at which two lineages separate; neither lineage is more advanced than the other.
A node represents a hypothetical common ancestor: the point at which the lineages arising from it diverged. All the organisms on the branches beyond a node form a clade.
A student who thinks cladistics assigns Linnaean ranks picks this. Clades are unranked; a node marks a common ancestor and defines a clade, but it does not correspond to any rank.

mcqs.q: On a cladogram, the root leads to node 1, where species P branches off. Node 2 separates species Q from the remaining species. Node 3 separates species R from species S and T, which are joined at node 4. Which statement is correct?
options: Q is more closely related to R than to T, because Q and R branch at adjacent nodes.
P is the most primitive of the five species, because it branches off nearest the root.
Q, R and S form a clade, and so do Q, R, S and T taken together as a group.
R shares a more recent common ancestor with S than it shares with Q.
mcqs.explain: R's lineage joins the S–T lineage at node 3, whereas it joins Q's lineage further back at node 2. The common ancestor at node 3 is more recent than the one at node 2, so R is more closely related to S than to Q.
rationales: A student who judges relatedness by adjacency picks this. Q's lineage separates at node 2 from the lineage leading to R, S and T together, so Q shares the same common ancestor with R as with T and is equally related to all three.

A student who reads early branching as primitiveness picks this. P's lineage separated first, but it has been evolving for as long as the others since the root; a cladogram shows branching order, not degree of advancement.

A student who treats any convenient grouping as a clade picks this. Q, R, S and T are all the descendants of the ancestor at node 2 and do form a clade, but Q, R and S without T omit a descendant of that ancestor, so they do not.

R's lineage joins the S–T lineage at node 3, whereas it joins Q's lineage further back at node 2. The common ancestor at node 3 is more recent than the one at node 2, so R is more closely related to S than to Q.

mcqs.q: Several genera were placed in the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae) because of similarities in flower structure. Cladistic analysis of base sequences later showed that some of these genera are more closely related to plants in other families than to the remaining figworts, and they were transferred out of the family. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The floral similarities arose by convergent evolution, so the family was not a clade and its original classification has been falsified.
The transferred genera must still share an ancestor with the figworts, because such similar flowers could not have evolved twice.
Flower structure is directly observable and so more reliable than sequences, which makes the transfer premature.
The original family should be retained, because an established classification is not overturned by later evidence.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cladistics can show a classification is wrong
mcqs.explain: Similarities in morphology due to convergent evolution rather than common ancestry suggested a classification that cladistics has shown to be false. The sequence evidence shows that the family did not correspond to evolutionary relationships, illustrating that scientific knowledge claims may eventually be falsified.
rationales: Similarities in morphology due to convergent evolution rather than common ancestry suggested a classification that cladistics has shown to be false. The sequence evidence shows that the family did not correspond to evolutionary relationships, illustrating that scientific knowledge claims may eventually be falsified.

A student who assumes a specialized structure cannot evolve independently picks this. Convergent evolution can produce similar flowers in unrelated lineages, and the sequence evidence shows that this is what happened here.
A student who trusts morphology over molecular data picks this. Base sequences are the most objective evidence of common ancestry, and it was the morphological classification that proved misleading.
A student who regards classifications as settled facts picks this. Classifications are scientific knowledge claims that may be falsified, and the reclassification is a direct example of that process.

mcqs.q: Which evidence was used in 1977 to propose that all organisms should be classified into three domains?
options: Visible differences in cell structure seen using the electron microscope.
Comparison of the base sequences of ribosomal RNA across many different organisms.
Evidence that archaea are a subgroup of bacteria, so that all prokaryotes form one domain.
Overall similarity in the appearance and way of life of the organisms being classified.
mcqs.specStatementText: Three domains, from ribosomal RNA sequences
mcqs.explain: The classification of all organisms into three domains was proposed in 1977 using evidence from rRNA base sequences, which showed that prokaryotes fall into two groups as different from each other as either is from eukaryotes.
rationales: A student who assumes every division of life is based on visible cell structure picks this. Archaea and bacteria are not distinguishable by cell structure alone; it was rRNA sequence comparison that revealed the split.

The classification of all organisms into three domains was proposed in 1977 using evidence from rRNA base sequences, which showed that prokaryotes fall into two groups as different from each other as either is from eukaryotes.

A student who takes archaea to be unusual bacteria picks this. The 1977 proposal rested on rRNA base sequences, which showed that Archaea and Bacteria are as different from each other as either is from Eukarya, so they were placed in separate domains (A3.2.9).
A student who thinks classification rests on resemblance picks this. Overall similarity gives no basis for separating archaea from bacteria; the domains rest on rRNA sequence evidence.

mcqs.q: The rRNA base sequences of an archaean are found to differ from those of bacteria as much as they differ from those of eukaryotes. Which classification does this evidence support?
options: Archaea placed within the domain Bacteria, since both groups lack a nucleus.
Archaea as a sixth kingdom, the highest level of classification.
Archaea as a separate domain, distinct from both Bacteria and Eukarya.
Archaea grouped with bacteria, because cell structure outweighs rRNA evidence.
mcqs.specStatementText: Three domains, from ribosomal RNA sequences
mcqs.explain: If archaeal rRNA differs from bacterial rRNA as much as from eukaryotic rRNA, the three groups are separated by divergences of similar depth, which supports three domains, Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, at a level above the kingdoms.
rationales: A student who takes archaea to be unusual bacteria picks this. Lacking a nucleus is shared by both groups, but the rRNA evidence shows they are as far apart as either is from eukaryotes, which is inconsistent with one domain containing both.

A student who thinks domain is just another name for kingdom picks this. The domains are an extra level above the kingdoms; the evidence places archaea at that highest level, not as a kingdom alongside plants and animals.

If archaeal rRNA differs from bacterial rRNA as much as from eukaryotic rRNA, the three groups are separated by divergences of similar depth, which supports three domains, Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, at a level above the kingdoms.

A student who expects classification to follow visible cell structure picks this. The three-domain classification was proposed from rRNA base sequences precisely because cell structure does not reveal the depth of the split between archaea and bacteria.

mcqs.q: What is the main advantage of a classification in which every group corresponds to evolutionary relationships?
options: The groups show which of the organisms are the most advanced.
Every species is given a unique name made up of two parts.
Organisms that look alike are placed together for identification.
Characteristics of members of a group can be predicted.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why grouping by ancestry is the ideal
mcqs.explain: When all the members of a taxonomic group have evolved from a common ancestor, characteristics of organisms within the group can be predicted because they are shared within the clade.
rationales: A student who sees evolutionary classification as a ranking from primitive to advanced picks this. Groups based on common ancestry make no claim that any living species is more advanced than another.
A student who thinks classification is about naming picks this. Species are named whatever the basis of the classification; the advantage of following evolutionary relationships is predictive.

A student who thinks classification is by resemblance picks this. Grouping by evolutionary relationships sometimes separates organisms that look alike and unites ones that look different; its advantage is that inherited characteristics can be predicted.
When all the members of a taxonomic group have evolved from a common ancestor, characteristics of organisms within the group can be predicted because they are shared within the clade.

mcqs.q: The same protein in two living species differs at 8 amino acid positions. Substitutions in this protein occur at about 1 per 5 million years in each lineage. Which is the best estimate of the time since the two species diverged from their common ancestor?
options: About 20 million years, since roughly half of the differences have accumulated in each of the two lineages.
About 40 million years, because 8 substitutions at 5 million years each took 40 million years to occur.
Exactly 20 million years, because the substitution rate is the same in every lineage at all times.
It cannot be estimated, because the fossil ancestor at the node has not been found and sequenced.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sequence differences accumulate, so they estimate divergence time
mcqs.explain: Sequence differences accumulate gradually in both lineages after divergence, so the 8 differences are shared between the two lineages, about 4 each, and 4 × 5 million years gives an estimate of 20 million years. It is only an estimate, because the rate is affected by generation time, population size, selective pressure and other factors.
rationales: Sequence differences accumulate gradually in both lineages after divergence, so the 8 differences are shared between the two lineages, about 4 each, and 4 × 5 million years gives an estimate of 20 million years. It is only an estimate, because the rate is affected by generation time, population size, selective pressure and other factors.

A student who attributes all the differences to one lineage picks this. Both lineages accumulated substitutions after they separated, so the 8 differences represent about 4 per lineage, giving 4 × 5 = 20 million years.

A student who takes the molecular clock to be exact picks this. The arithmetic is right, but the clock can only give estimates: mutation rates vary with generation time, population size, selective pressure and other factors.

A student who thinks a node is an identified fossil ancestor whose sequence is needed picks this. The estimate uses the differences between the two living species; a node represents a hypothetical common ancestor inferred from the data, and its sequence is not required.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The figwort (Scrophulariaceae) reclassification is used only as the guide describes it: a family defined by floral morphology that cladistic analysis of sequences showed was not a clade, with genera transferred to other families. The item on this statement supplies the outline of the case in its stem and tests the reasoning (convergent evolution, falsification), so no item requires recall of which genera were moved, to which families, or the year of the study.
